title: Equitable queueing for KV-aware hybrid batching
content:
Purpose and framing:

This is a working sketch for a hybrid batching scheduler that balances token-level efficiency with request-level fairness while remaining KV-cache friendly and kernel-aware. Goal is to design a practical policy that: (1) preserves overall throughput by exploiting token coalescing and kernel favorable shapes, (2) prevents starvation and poor tail latency for low-volume or long-running requests, and (3) keeps KV cache locality high to avoid repeated cache population churn.

Why we need something new:
- Pure token-level coalescing maximizes GPU utilization but can starve rare or long requests (head-of-line blocking when short requests keep arriving).
- Pure request-level fairness (serve whole requests in FIFO/round-robin) offers predictability but loses batching opportunities and increases per-token cost.
- KV cache behavior couples with batching granularity: scattering tokens from many requests reduces hit rates and increases effective memory pressure.
- Kernel selection (e.g., fused attention vs. memory-optimized kernels) benefits from predictable sequence-length distributions; mixing many different lengths harms kernel performance and launch overheads.

High-level approach: hybrid queueing with dynamic granularity
- Maintain two logical queues per worker: a fairness queue (RQ) of pending requests and a token coalescing pool (TP) of ready tokens available for immediate microbatches.
- On arrival, a request is registered in RQ with metadata: remaining_tokens, priority_score (compute below), kv_affinity_tag, model_variant_hint, created_at.
- Scheduler runs at micro-epoch ticks (configurable 1-5 ms). Each tick:
  1) Inspect RQ head(s) and TP pool.
  2) Decide whether to drain a request from RQ (serve request-level chunk) or pull tokens from TP to form a token-level microbatch. Decision is based on a score function that mixes fairness deficit and batch utility.

Score components (all normalized to [0,1]):
- Fairness deficit F_r = min(1, target_share_r - produced_share_r). Target_share_r derived from weight (e.g., plan/capacity or SLA class) and time window. Produced_share_r is past service fraction. This enforces long-term proportional fairness.
- Latency urgency U_r = sigmoid((p99_target - observed_latency_r) / scale). Captures per-request SLA pressure.
- Batch utility B_pool = estimated_token_coalescing_gain(token_set) — predicts per-token GPU efficiency for assembling a microbatch from TP at this tick. Estimation uses kernel profiles: if tokens have similar sequence lengths and kv_affinity, B_pool high.
- KV affinity penalty K_penalty = 1 - kv_locality_score(token_set). We penalize strategies that would lower kv hit rate significantly.

Decision rule (simplified):
- If max_r (alpha * F_r + beta * U_r) > gamma * B_pool - delta * K_penalty, then pick request-level drain for that r; else form a token-level microbatch from TP.
- alpha/beta/gamma/delta are tunable weights set per-deployment (defaults: alpha=0.6, beta=0.3, gamma=0.9, delta=0.8).

Practical scheduling primitives
- Request chunking: When draining a request, we can either: a) drain until completion, b) drain up to max_chunk_tokens (e.g., 64 tokens) then re-enqueue. Default: chunk to min(remaining, max_chunk_tokens) so long requests don't hog GPU.
- Token microbatch formation: select tokens greedily by kv_affinity_tag and sequence length bucket to maximize kernel fit. If microbatch size < min_effective_batch (e.g., 8 tokens), optionally wait up to microbatch_timeout (config), or fill with lower-utility tokens marked as opportunistic.
- KV affinity tagging: assign each request a tag based on recent KV keyset (e.g., conversation id, user id hash) to prefer grouping tokens from same tag. Maintain counters to estimate hit rate from tag locality.

KV-cache awareness and heuristics
- Affinity-first selection: when forming token batches, prefer tokens with same kv_affinity_tag to preserve cache locality. If the best tag pool is small, weigh the tradeoff between waiting for more tokens and falling back to mixed-tag batches.
- Cache-warm hints: when a request is drained via request-level chunk (not token coalesced), we mark its kv keys as warmed to reduce future penalty if later token coalescing occurs.
- Eviction-friendly scheduling: detect when evictions are occurring too frequently (measured by per-request cache-miss spikes) and bias batches to restore locality.

Kernel selection coordination
- Keep short sequence-length buckets and long sequence-length buckets separate when forming token microbatches. Predict kernel choice at scheduling time and compute B_pool accordingly using microbenchmarks (we have a small lookup table for model-arch x seq-length -> per-token throughput).
- When kernels are unstable (mixed lengths cause kernel fallback), favor request-level drains to keep kernel runs homogeneous.

Fairness formalization and targets
- Primary fairness objective: long-term proportional share across SLA classes (guaranteed fraction of GPU time). Implement via deficit counters (like deficit round-robin) updated per-token serviced.
- Short-term latency fairness: ensure no request waits longer than max_inflight_wait_ms (e.g., 150 ms) without being served some tokens. Enforced via urgency kick that raises U_r rapidly after threshold.
- Starvation protection: any request older than starvation_threshold receives immediate priority for the next slot.

Metrics to track (per-worker + aggregated):
- Throughput: tokens/sec, requests/sec.
- Cost-efficiency: tokens/sec per GPU, percent of microbatches using optimal kernel.
- Latency: mean, p50/p90/p95/p99 request completion and per-token latencies.
- Fairness: per-SLA token share vs. target over sliding windows (1s, 10s, 5m).
- KV metrics: cache hit rate, miss rate, warmed-tags ratio, eviction frequency.
- Scheduling dynamics: fraction of time we pick request-level vs token-level, average microbatch size, avg kv-affinity within batch.

Simulation plan and microbenchmarks
- Offline sim harness: replay traces (we have traces from prod: trace-jan2024-longtails, trace-aug2024-chat-bursts). Implement policy knobs and compute above metrics.
- Microbench kernels: measure actual per-token throughput for relevant (model,seq_len) combos on target GPU images; produce lookup tables for scheduler.
- Ablations: vary alpha/beta/gamma/delta, max_chunk_tokens, microbatch_timeout, min_effective_batch. Evaluate throughput vs fairness vs p99.

API surface and config examples
- Per-queue config options (YAML-like):
  scheduler:
    tick_ms: 3
    max_chunk_tokens: 64
    microbatch_timeout_ms: 6
    min_effective_batch: 8
    weights:
      fairness_alpha: 0.6
      urgency_beta: 0.3
      pool_gamma: 0.9
      kv_delta: 0.8
    starvation_threshold_ms: 200
    kv:
      enable_affinity_grouping: true
      affinity_bucket_count: 128
- Runtime introspection endpoints: /metrics/scheduler_state, /debug/samples (last N scheduling decisions).

Implementation notes and complexity risks
- State volume: per-worker correlation maps for kv tags could be large; use probabilistic counters (Count-Min / HyperLogLog) for tag prevalence estimates.
- Clock skew and fairness windows: maintain token-service counters with monotonic time; avoid per-request floating-window heavy state. Use bucketed counters.
- Stability: tuning knobs interact—automate moderate default values and ship experiments behind feature flags.
- Overhead: scheduling decision must be cheap (<~200ns path if possible). Precompute B_pool heuristics and cache token-set aggregates to avoid scanning entire TP each tick.

Open questions and TODOs
- How to best compute target_share_r for ephemeral requests? (per-customer commit vs per-SLA-class?) Proposal: default by SLA class, allow explicit per-customer capacity allocations via config.
- Best evictions signals to correlate with batch decisions? Track eviction latency spikes and expose to scheduler as a soft constraint.
- Do we want to persist kv-affinity tags across worker restarts? Probably yes for longer conversational sessions — design lightweight persistent tag registry.
- Explore machine-learned B_pool estimators if lookup tables prove insufficient.

Next steps (near-term experiment roadmap)
1) Implement basic version: RQ + TP data structures, chunking, simple score rule with default weights. Feature flag roll-out to internal canary pool. (owner: Arjun)
2) Collect production traces and compute baseline metrics (owner: Lena).
3) Tune weights via grid search in offline sim and pick two candidate configs to A/B in canary. (owner: Maya)
4) Add KV affinity heuristics and cache-warm hints; measure KV hit rate improvements. (owner: Samir)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conversational and contains many heuristics — please point out known pitfalls from prior schedulers (e.g., stability issues with deficit counters in bursty workloads).
- If you have concrete kernel throughput numbers for any model we ship, paste them in and I will fold into B_pool estimators.

Appendix: quick pseudocode sketch (very high level)

for each tick:
  update_B_pool_estimate()
  candidate_r = head_of_RQ()
  score_r = alpha * fairness_deficit(candidate_r) + beta * urgency(candidate_r)
  if score_r > gamma * B_pool - delta * kv_penalty_for_top_pool():
    serve_chunk(candidate_r, size=min(candidate_r.remaining, max_chunk_tokens))
  else:
    batch = form_token_microbatch(prefer_by_kv=true, prefer_same_length=true)
    if batch.size >= min_effective_batch or waited_long_enough(batch.tokens):
      dispatch(batch)
    else:
      optionally_wait_or_force_dispatch()

(End of sketch)

-- Maya

References / related notes:
- See GH PR 3124 for initial simpler token-only coalescer that this extends.
- Related design docs in Drive: microbatch-scheduler-token-fairness-draft.json (useful baselines), continuous-batcher-design-notes-token-level-vs-request-level.json (high-level comparisons). This doc intentionally focuses on hybridization and KV affinity mechanics.
